newsitem.title: USA: China's defense chief to visit U.S.
newsitem.headline: China's defense chief to visit U.S.

text.p: In a sign of improving relations between Washington and Beijing, the Pentagon announced on Monday that Chinese Defence Minister Chi Haotian will visit the United States for two weeks next month.

The statement said Gen. Chi and a 20-member senior delegation from China's defence and foreign ministries will arrive Dec. 5 and hold talks in Washington with Defence Secretary William Perry and U.S. officials. Perry visited China in October 1994.

Chi had been scheduled to visit Washington last March, but both countries called off the visit at that time because of high tension between the two powers over U.S. charges of Chinese sabre-rattling to influence elections in Taiwan.

The Clinton administration and Chinese leaders have, however, moved to improve ties in recent weeks, including a visit to China by Secretary of State Warren Christopher and talks between President Bill Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin on Sunday at a meeting of Asia-Pacific leaders in the Philippines.

"The objectives of this (Chi) visit are to exchange views on global and Asia-Pacific regional security issues of mutual concern and to discuss future prospects for bilateral military relations," the Pentagon statement said.

Despite trade disputes and U.S. concern over human rights in China and reports that China may have provided nuclear technology to Pakistan and Iran, the Pentagon said Chi would travel to several U.S. military bases.
He will wind up his trip with talks at the U.S. Pacific Command in Hawaii Dec. 16-18.
The Pentagon said that the full schedule for Chi's trip was still being worked out.

Perry, who has announced that he will resign his post after nearly three years on the job as soon as Clinton finds a replacement, has stressed repeatedly that the United States cannot ignore China despite problems over their sometimes-conflicting policies.

"The visit will provide an opportunity to increase senior Chinese military leaders' understanding of U.S. national security policies, armed forces and, more broadly, American society," the Pentagon statement said.
